questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a load balancer?

options.text: To encrypt traffic between clients and servers
To distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers
To cache frequently accessed content at the edge
To compress response data for faster transmission

questions.explanation: Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple backend servers to improve availability, reliability, and scalability. Netflix uses load balancers to distribute traffic across thousands of servers. While modern load balancers may also handle SSL termination or basic caching, traffic distribution is the primary function. Without load balancing, you can't horizontally scale web applications.

questions.question: A load balancer detects that one of five backend servers is unhealthy. What should happen to traffic destined for that server?

options.text: Traffic continues to the unhealthy server until manual intervention
Traffic is redistributed to healthy servers
All traffic stops until the server recovers
The load balancer shuts down to prevent errors

questions.explanation: Load balancers perform health checks and automatically remove unhealthy servers from the pool, redistributing their traffic to healthy servers. This is fundamental to high availability—users don't experience errors when servers fail. AWS ELB, Nginx, and HAProxy all implement automatic health-based routing. The unhealthy server is re-added when health checks pass again.

questions.question: Which are benefits of using a load balancer? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Improved availability through redundancy
Horizontal scaling capability
Automatic code deployment to servers
SSL termination offloading

questions.explanation: Load balancers enable high availability (traffic shifts from failed servers automatically), horizontal scaling (add servers behind LB without client changes), and SSL offloading (decrypt at LB, reducing backend CPU load). Code deployment is a CI/CD function handled by tools like Jenkins, ArgoCD, or AWS CodeDeploy—not load balancers. Cloudflare terminates SSL for millions of sites at their edge.

questions.question: What is the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?

options.text: Layer 4 is faster; Layer 7 provides better security
Layer 4 routes by IP/port; Layer 7 routes by application data (HTTP headers, URLs)
Layer 4 is for TCP only; Layer 7 is for UDP only
Layer 4 requires more expensive hardware

questions.explanation: Layer 4 (transport) LBs make decisions based on TCP/UDP port and IP address—fast but limited. Layer 7 (application) LBs understand HTTP and can route based on URL paths (/api vs /static), headers, cookies, or request content. AWS NLB is Layer 4; ALB is Layer 7. Use L4 for raw performance (gaming, databases); use L7 for intelligent routing (microservices, A/B testing).

questions.question: A web application requires that a user's session always goes to the same backend server. Which load balancer feature enables this?

options.text: Round-robin distribution algorithm
Session persistence / sticky sessions
Active health checking
SSL termination

questions.explanation: Session persistence (sticky sessions) ensures requests from the same client go to the same server, typically using cookies or source IP hashing. This is needed when session state is stored locally on servers (not recommended but common in legacy apps). AWS ALB supports sticky sessions via cookies. Better approach: externalize session state to Redis, eliminating the need for stickiness.

questions.question: What is a potential drawback of sticky sessions?

options.text: Increased network latency for all requests
Uneven load distribution if some users are more active
Incompatibility with HTTPS connections
Requires more backend servers than non-sticky

questions.explanation: Sticky sessions can cause uneven load—if heavy users (power users, bots) are stuck to certain servers, those servers become overloaded while others sit idle. It also complicates server removal during deployments or failures (stuck users lose sessions). Shopify moved away from sticky sessions to stateless architecture for better scalability and simpler operations.

questions.question: A load balancer is configured with active health checks. What does this mean?

options.text: It monitors server CPU and memory usage
It periodically sends requests to servers to verify they're healthy
It only checks health when a real request fails
It relies on servers to self-report their health status

questions.explanation: Active health checks proactively probe backend servers (HTTP GET to /health, TCP connect, etc.) at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 seconds). Passive checks only detect failures when real requests fail. Active checks catch problems before users are affected. AWS ELB health checks can verify HTTP 200 responses, check specific paths, and configure thresholds for marking unhealthy.

questions.question: True or False: A single load balancer can become a single point of failure.

options.text: True - load balancers need redundancy too
False - load balancers are inherently fault-tolerant

questions.explanation: A single load balancer is indeed a SPOF—if it fails, all traffic stops regardless of healthy backends. Production environments use redundant load balancers: active-passive (failover) or active-active (both serving traffic). AWS ELB is itself distributed across AZs. For on-premise, use keepalived/VRRP for LB failover. Always design for LB redundancy in production.

questions.question: Which load balancer configuration provides the highest availability?

options.text: Single load balancer with powerful hardware
Active-passive load balancer pair with failover
Active-active load balancer cluster with DNS failover
Load balancer with frequent configuration backups

questions.explanation: Active-active clusters distribute load across multiple LBs simultaneously and handle failover automatically—no single point of failure, no failover delay. Active-passive has failover delay while the passive LB takes over. Single LB is a SPOF regardless of hardware. Backups don't provide runtime redundancy. Cloudflare and AWS use active-active globally distributed load balancing.

questions.question: A company uses a cloud load balancer that automatically scales based on traffic. What type of load balancer is this?

options.text: Hardware load balancer appliance
Software load balancer on VMs
Managed/elastic load balancer
DNS-based load balancer

questions.explanation: Managed/elastic load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Load Balancer, Azure Load Balancer) automatically scale capacity based on traffic, abstracting infrastructure management. You don't provision instances or worry about LB capacity—the cloud provider handles it. This is why cloud-native architectures prefer managed LBs over self-managed Nginx/HAProxy for most use cases.

questions.question: What happens during a 'connection draining' or 'deregistration delay' when removing a server from a load balancer?

options.text: All connections are immediately terminated
Existing connections complete while new connections go elsewhere
The server is kept in the pool indefinitely
Traffic is duplicated to both old and new servers

questions.explanation: Connection draining allows in-flight requests to complete gracefully (typically 30-300 seconds) while stopping new requests to the server being removed. This prevents request failures during deployments, scaling events, or maintenance. AWS calls this 'deregistration delay'; Kubernetes uses 'terminationGracePeriodSeconds'. Essential for zero-downtime deployments.

questions.question: Which scenarios require Layer 7 load balancing instead of Layer 4? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Routing based on URL path (/api vs /web)
Simple TCP port-based distribution
A/B testing based on cookies or headers
Routing based on HTTP headers (API version, content type)

questions.explanation: URL path routing (/api to API servers, /static to CDN), cookie-based A/B testing, and header inspection all require Layer 7 understanding of HTTP. Simple port-based distribution (all traffic on port 443 to any backend) works at Layer 4. Istio and Envoy provide sophisticated L7 routing for microservices. Use L7 when you need content-aware routing decisions.
